subclauses.title: Understanding the organization and its context
subclauses.summary: Identify internal and external issues that affect the ability of the ISMS to achieve its outcomes. A 2024 amendment added that climate change must be considered as a possible relevant issue.

subclauses.title: Needs and expectations of interested parties
subclauses.summary: Identify interested parties, their relevant requirements, and which of those the ISMS will address. The 2024 amendment notes that interested parties can have climate-related requirements.

subclauses.title: Determining the scope of the ISMS
subclauses.summary: Set the boundaries of the ISMS using 4.1, 4.2, and the interfaces and dependencies with other organisations. The scope must be documented.

subclauses.title: Information security management system
subclauses.summary: Establish, implement, maintain and continually improve the ISMS, including the processes it needs and how they interact.

subclauses.title: Leadership and commitment
subclauses.summary: Top management must show commitment, for example by aligning the policy with strategy, integrating the ISMS into business processes, providing resources and supporting other managers.

subclauses.title: Policy
subclauses.summary: Top management sets an information security policy that suits the organisation's purpose, includes or frames objectives, commits to meeting requirements and to continual improvement. It must be documented, communicated and available to interested parties as appropriate.

subclauses.title: Organizational roles, responsibilities and authorities
subclauses.summary: Top management makes sure responsibilities and authorities for security-relevant roles are assigned and communicated. It must specifically assign who ensures the ISMS conforms to the standard and who reports ISMS performance to top management.

subclauses.title: Actions to address risks and opportunities: general
subclauses.summary: Plan actions for risks and opportunities so the ISMS achieves its outcomes, prevents undesired effects and improves continually.

subclauses.title: Information security risk assessment
subclauses.summary: Define and apply a risk assessment process with criteria for risk acceptance and for performing assessments. Repeated assessments must give consistent, valid and comparable results. Identify risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability, assign risk owners, analyse consequences and likelihood, determine risk levels and evaluate against criteria. Keep the process documented.

subclauses.title: Information security risk treatment
subclauses.summary: Choose treatment options, determine the necessary controls, compare them with Annex A so nothing is missed, produce a Statement of Applicability, write a risk treatment plan, and get risk owners to approve the plan and accept residual risk. Keep the process documented.

subclauses.title: Information security objectives and planning to achieve them
subclauses.summary: Set measurable (where practicable) objectives consistent with the policy, monitored, communicated and updated. Plan what will be done, resources, who is responsible, completion dates and how results are evaluated.

subclauses.title: Planning of changes
subclauses.summary: New in 2022. Changes to the ISMS must be carried out in a planned way.

subclauses.title: Resources
subclauses.summary: Provide the resources needed for the ISMS.

subclauses.title: Competence
subclauses.summary: Determine required competence, ensure people are competent through education, training or experience, take action to close gaps, and keep evidence of competence.

subclauses.title: Awareness
subclauses.summary: People working under the organisation's control must know the policy, their contribution to the ISMS, and the consequences of not conforming.

subclauses.title: Communication
subclauses.summary: Decide what to communicate, when, with whom and how.

subclauses.title: Documented information
subclauses.summary: Include documented information required by the standard and that the organisation decides it needs. Control creation, updating, identification, format, review, approval, distribution, access, storage, version control, retention and disposal, including external documents.

subclauses.title: Operational planning and control
subclauses.summary: Plan, implement and control the processes needed, set criteria for them, control planned changes, review unintended changes, and control externally provided processes, products or services relevant to the ISMS.

subclauses.title: Information security risk assessment
subclauses.summary: Perform risk assessments at planned intervals and when significant changes occur. Keep the results.

subclauses.title: Information security risk treatment
subclauses.summary: Implement the risk treatment plan. Keep the results.

subclauses.title: Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation
subclauses.summary: Decide what to monitor and measure, methods, when, who does it, and when and by whom results are analysed and evaluated. Keep evidence of results.

subclauses.title: Internal audit
subclauses.summary: Run audits at planned intervals to check the ISMS conforms to the organisation's own requirements and the standard, and is effectively implemented. Plan an audit programme, define criteria and scope, pick objective and impartial auditors, report results to management, and keep evidence.

subclauses.title: Management review
subclauses.summary: Top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals. Inputs include status of previous actions, changes in issues and interested party needs, performance feedback (nonconformities, monitoring results, audit results, objectives), interested party feedback, risk assessment results and treatment status, and improvement opportunities. Outputs include improvement decisions and any changes needed. Keep evidence.

subclauses.title: Continual improvement
subclauses.summary: Continually improve the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the ISMS. In the 2022 edition this subclause comes first.

subclauses.title: Nonconformity and corrective action
subclauses.summary: React to the nonconformity, control and correct it, deal with consequences, find the root cause, check whether similar issues exist or could occur, implement actions, review their effectiveness and change the ISMS if needed. Keep evidence of the nonconformity, actions taken and results.

mandatory_documented_information.note: Treated as mandatory by most certification bodies. The standard explicitly requires documented information on the treatment process and its results.

mandatory_documented_information.item: Documented information the organisation decides is necessary
Evidence that processes have been carried out as planned
Nonconformities, actions taken and corrective action results

attributes_iso27002.operational_capabilities_note: Fifteen capabilities such as governance, asset management, identity and access management, threat and vulnerability management

key_concepts.definition: Information is not made available or disclosed to unauthorised people, entities or processes.
Information is accurate and complete.
Information is accessible and usable on demand by an authorised entity.
Policies, procedures, guidelines and the related resources and activities, managed together by an organisation to protect its information assets (ISO/IEC 27000).
Effect of uncertainty on objectives. Often expressed as a combination of consequence and likelihood.
Person or entity with the accountability and authority to manage a risk.
Risk remaining after risk treatment.
The level of risk the organisation is prepared to accept. Set in the risk criteria under 6.1.2.

Commonly taught as four options: modify (apply controls), retain (accept), avoid, and share (for example insurance). ISO/IEC 27005:2018 had a subclause for each. The 2022 edition replaced these with one general clause on selecting treatment options, but sharing and retention remain defined terms.
Document listing the necessary controls, justification for including them, whether they are implemented, and justification for excluding any Annex A controls.
Non-fulfilment of a requirement.
Correction fixes the immediate problem. Corrective action removes the root cause to stop it recurring.
Person or organisation that can affect, be affected by, or think itself affected by a decision or activity.
Person or group that directs and controls the organisation at the highest level.
Information an organisation must control and maintain, and the medium holding it. Replaces the older terms documents and records.
The common clause structure (formerly Annex SL) shared by ISO management system standards such as 27001, 9001, 14001 and 42001. Makes integration easier.
Plan-Do-Check-Act. ISO 27001:2022 does not require or mention PDCA. By common training convention, clauses 4 to 6 map to Plan, 7 to 8 to Do, 9 to Check and 10 to Act.
Certification body reviews documentation and readiness, including scope, policy, risk process and SoA.
Certification body checks the ISMS is implemented and effective in practice.
Annual audits in years two and three of the certification cycle.
Full re-audit before the three-year certificate expires.

Annex A went from 114 controls in 14 domains to 93 controls in 4 themes. 11 controls are new. Clause 6.3 Planning of changes was added. The transition period for certified organisations ended on 31 October 2025.

lessons_note: Lesson text is paraphrased study material written from Claude training data and checked against this pack. It is not the wording of ISO/IEC 27001 or 27002. Verify against the standard.

lessons.title: What information security protects
lessons.intro: Information security protects information from harm. This lesson covers the three properties every exam question builds on, and the basic language of risk.

sections.heading: Information is an asset
body: An asset is anything of value to the organisation. Information is an asset in any form: a database, a paper file, an email, or what an engineer knows about a system.

Information also depends on supporting assets, such as laptops, servers, networks, buildings, suppliers and people. ISO 27001:2022 calls these 'information and other associated assets'. If a supporting asset fails, the information it holds is at risk.

sections.heading: Confidentiality, integrity and availability
body: ISO/IEC 27000 describes information security as preserving three properties. Learn them so you can name the right one from a short scenario.
points: Confidentiality: only authorised people, entities or processes can see the information. A leaked customer list is a confidentiality failure.
Integrity: the information is accurate and complete. An unauthorised change to payroll figures is an integrity failure.
Availability: authorised users can access and use the information when they need it. A server outage or ransomware that locks files is an availability failure.

sections.heading: Other properties
body: ISO/IEC 27000 notes that other properties can also be involved, such as authenticity, accountability, non-repudiation and reliability. Exam options often include these as distractors. When a question asks which of the three core properties is affected, pick from confidentiality, integrity and availability.

sections.heading: Threat, vulnerability and risk
body: A threat is a possible cause of an unwanted incident, such as a phishing campaign or a flood. A vulnerability is a weakness a threat can exploit, such as an unpatched server or staff who have never had phishing training.

Risk arises when a threat can exploit a vulnerability and affect an asset. ISO defines risk as the effect of uncertainty on objectives. In practice you express it as a combination of the likelihood of an event and its consequence.

example.title: Which property?
example.text: A hospital's patient system goes down for six hours. No data is lost or copied. Clinicians cannot see records. Only availability is affected. If an attacker had also downloaded the records, confidentiality would be affected too. If they had changed medication doses, integrity would be affected.

exam_tips: Read scenario questions for the effect, not the cause. Ransomware is usually an availability question unless the scenario says data was stolen.
Unauthorised change means integrity. Unauthorised disclosure means confidentiality.

lessons.title: What an ISMS is and the ISO 27000 family
lessons.intro: An ISMS is how an organisation manages information security as a system rather than as a set of separate tools. This lesson explains the idea and the standards around it.

sections.heading: The ISMS idea
body: ISO/IEC 27000 describes an ISMS as policies, procedures, guidelines, and the related resources and activities, managed together to protect information assets.

The key word is managed. An ISMS sets direction from top management, assesses risk, chooses controls to match that risk, checks they work, and improves over time. A firewall on its own is a control. An ISMS is the system that decides you need the firewall, owns it and checks it.
points: It is risk based: controls follow from assessed risk.
It is led from the top: top management sets policy and provides resources.
It improves: results are measured, reviewed and acted on.

sections.heading: Requirements versus guidance
body: ISO/IEC 27001 is the requirements standard. Its requirements use the word 'shall'. It is the only standard in the family that an organisation can be certified against.
Most of the rest of the family is guidance. Guidance helps you meet the requirements but you are not audited against it.

sections.heading: The standards you need to know
points: ISO/IEC 27000: overview and vocabulary. The source of definitions.
ISO/IEC 27001: ISMS requirements, including Annex A.
ISO/IEC 27002: guidance on each Annex A control.
ISO/IEC 27003: guidance on clauses 4 to 10.
ISO/IEC 27004: guidance on monitoring and measurement.
ISO/IEC 27005: guidance on information security risk management.
ISO/IEC 27006-1: requirements for certification bodies.
ISO/IEC 27007: guidance on auditing an ISMS, building on ISO 19011.
ISO/IEC 27017 and 27018: cloud security and protection of personal data in public cloud.
ISO/IEC 27701: privacy information management.

sections.heading: The harmonized structure
body: ISO management system standards share a common clause structure, formerly called Annex SL. ISO 9001, ISO 14001, ISO 27001 and ISO 42001 all use clauses 4 to 10 in the same order with similar core text. This makes it easier to run one integrated management system.

sections.heading: Laws, regulations and best practice
body: An ISMS sits alongside the law. Data protection law, such as the UK GDPR, sector regulation and contracts all create requirements. ISO 27001 expects you to identify these as interested party requirements (clause 4.2) and to meet them (control 5.31). Certification does not prove legal compliance on its own.

example.title: Picking the right standard
example.text: A consultant asks where to find the definition of 'residual risk'. The answer is ISO/IEC 27000. A client asks how to implement control 8.24 Use of cryptography. The answer is ISO/IEC 27002. A certification body asks what rules it must follow to certify an ISMS. The answer is ISO/IEC 27006-1.

exam_tips: If an option says you can be certified to 27002, it is wrong.
27006 is for certification bodies. 27007 is guidance for auditors. Exams test this pair often.

lessons.title: How ISO 27001:2022 is structured
lessons.intro: Before you study each clause, learn the shape of the standard. Most clause-number questions become easy once you know the map.

sections.heading: Clauses 0 to 3
body: Clause 0 is the introduction. Clause 1 is scope, clause 2 is normative references and clause 3 is terms and definitions, which points to ISO/IEC 27000. These clauses contain no requirements you are audited against.

sections.heading: Clauses 4 to 10: the requirements
points: 4 Context of the organization: issues, interested parties, scope.
5 Leadership: commitment, policy, roles.
6 Planning: risk assessment, risk treatment, objectives, planning of changes.
7 Support: resources, competence, awareness, communication, documented information.
8 Operation: run the processes, repeat risk assessment, carry out risk treatment.
9 Performance evaluation: monitoring, internal audit, management review.
10 Improvement: continual improvement, nonconformity and corrective action.

sections.heading: PDCA as a memory aid
body: ISO 27001:2022 does not require or mention Plan-Do-Check-Act. Training courses still use it as a memory aid. Clauses 4 to 6 map to Plan, 7 and 8 to Do, 9 to Check and 10 to Act.

sections.heading: Annex A
body: Annex A lists 93 controls in four themes: organizational (37), people (8), physical (14) and technological (34). It is a reference list. You compare your chosen controls against it so nothing necessary is missed.

sections.heading: What changed in 2022
points: Annex A went from 114 controls in 14 domains to 93 controls in 4 themes. 11 controls are new.
Clause 6.3 Planning of changes was added.
Clause 10 was reordered: 10.1 is now continual improvement and 10.2 nonconformity and corrective action.
Amendment 1 in 2024 added climate change as a possible relevant issue in 4.1 and an interested party requirement in 4.2.
The transition period for certified organisations ended on 31 October 2025.

example.title: Using the map
example.text: A question asks which clause covers deciding who receives ISMS reports. Communication sits in Support, so look in clause 7. It is 7.4.

exam_tips: Learn the seven clause titles in order. Many questions only test which clause a topic sits in.
PDCA questions are about convention, not a requirement of the standard.

lessons.title: Clause 4: context and scope
lessons.intro: Clause 4 is where every ISMS starts. You understand the organisation and its environment, then draw the boundary of the ISMS.

sections.heading: 4.1 Internal and external issues
body: Identify issues that affect the ISMS's ability to achieve its intended outcomes. External issues include laws, the threat environment, market and technology change. Internal issues include culture, structure, capabilities and existing systems.
Since Amendment 1 (2024) you must also decide whether climate change is a relevant issue. Common tools here are PESTLE and SWOT analysis, but the standard does not require a specific tool.

sections.heading: 4.2 Interested parties
body: Identify the interested parties relevant to the ISMS, their relevant requirements, and which of those requirements the ISMS will address. The 2022 edition added that last step.
Interested parties include customers, regulators, staff, shareholders, suppliers and insurers. Their requirements can be legal, contractual or simply expectations.

sections.heading: 4.3 Scope
body: Define the boundaries and applicability of the ISMS. Consider the issues from 4.1, the requirements from 4.2, and the interfaces and dependencies between your activities and those of other organisations.

The scope must be available as documented information. A good scope statement names the organisation units, locations, services and key technology covered, and explains any boundary that might look odd to an auditor.

sections.heading: 4.4 The ISMS
body: Establish, implement, maintain and continually improve the ISMS, including the processes it needs and how they interact.

example.title: A scope statement
example.text: A software company with offices in Leeds and Manchester sets its scope as: 'The design, development, hosting and support of the payroll SaaS platform, delivered from the Leeds office and the cloud environment, including supporting HR and IT functions.' The Manchester sales office is excluded. The scope explains the interface: sales staff never access customer payroll data.

exam_tips: Scope inputs are 4.1, 4.2, and interfaces and dependencies. Expect a question on this.
Scope is mandatory documented information.

lessons.title: Clause 5: leadership
lessons.intro: Clause 5 makes top management responsible for the ISMS. It cannot be handed off entirely to the IT department.

sections.heading: 5.1 Leadership and commitment
body: Top management must show leadership. Examples in the standard include making sure the policy and objectives fit the organisation's strategy, building ISMS requirements into business processes, providing resources, communicating why security matters, making sure the ISMS achieves its outcomes, and supporting other managers in their roles.
Top management means the person or group who directs and controls the organisation at the highest level, such as the board or executive team.

sections.heading: 5.2 Policy
body: Top management sets the information security policy. It must suit the organisation's purpose, include objectives or a framework for setting them, commit to meeting applicable requirements, and commit to continual improvement.

The policy must be documented, communicated within the organisation and available to interested parties as appropriate. Topic-specific policies, such as access control or backup, sit under it and relate to control 5.1.

sections.heading: 5.3 Roles, responsibilities and authorities
body: Top management makes sure security roles are assigned and communicated. It must assign two things specifically: responsibility for making sure the ISMS conforms to ISO 27001, and responsibility for reporting ISMS performance to top management.
Top management can assign the work. It keeps the accountability.

example.title: Evidence of commitment
example.text: An auditor asks the CEO how they support the ISMS. Good evidence includes signed policy, a budget line for security, minutes of management reviews the CEO chaired, and objectives that appear in business plans. A CEO who says 'IT handles that' is a warning sign.

exam_tips: The policy is set by top management, not the CISO alone.
Look for 'assign responsibility and authority' as the 5.3 answer.

lessons.title: Clause 6: planning and risk
lessons.intro: Clause 6 is the heart of ISO 27001. It requires a repeatable risk assessment, a risk treatment process, a Statement of Applicability, objectives and planned changes.

sections.heading: 6.1.1 Risks and opportunities
body: When planning the ISMS, consider the issues from 4.1 and requirements from 4.2. Then plan actions for the risks and opportunities that could stop the ISMS achieving its outcomes. This is about risks to the ISMS itself, such as losing the project sponsor.

sections.heading: 6.1.2 Risk assessment
body: Define and apply a risk assessment process. It must:
points: Set risk criteria, including risk acceptance criteria and criteria for performing assessments.
Produce consistent, valid and comparable results when repeated.
Identify risks to confidentiality, integrity and availability within the scope.
Identify a risk owner for each risk.
Analyse the potential consequences and the realistic likelihood, and set risk levels.
Evaluate risks against the criteria and prioritise them for treatment.

sections.heading: 6.1.3 Risk treatment
body: Choose treatment options, determine all the controls needed, and compare them with Annex A to check nothing necessary is missed. Then produce a Statement of Applicability, write a risk treatment plan, and get risk owners to approve the plan and accept the residual risk.
Controls can come from any source. Annex A is a cross-check, not a mandatory menu.

sections.heading: 6.2 Objectives
body: Set information security objectives at relevant functions and levels. They must be consistent with the policy, measurable where practicable, take account of requirements and risk results, be monitored, communicated and updated. Plan what will be done, with what resources, by whom, by when, and how results will be evaluated.

sections.heading: 6.3 Planning of changes
body: New in 2022. When the ISMS needs to change, carry out the change in a planned way.

example.title: A measurable objective
example.text: Weak: 'Improve security awareness.' Strong: '95% of staff complete phishing awareness training by 31 March, and the click rate in quarterly phishing tests falls below 5% by year end.' The strong version says what, how much and by when, so it can be monitored.

exam_tips: Consistent, valid and comparable is a favourite exam phrase.
Risk owners approve the treatment plan and accept residual risk.
The two criteria in 6.1.2 are risk acceptance criteria and criteria for performing assessments.

lessons.title: Clause 7: support
lessons.intro: Clause 7 covers what the ISMS needs to run: people, skills, awareness, communication and controlled documents.

sections.heading: 7.1 Resources and 7.2 Competence
body: Provide the resources the ISMS needs. For competence, decide what competence each role affecting security needs, make sure people have it through education, training or experience, act to close gaps, and check those actions worked.
Keep documented evidence of competence, such as training records, certificates or CVs.

sections.heading: 7.3 Awareness
body: Everyone working under the organisation's control must be aware of three things:
points: The information security policy.
Their contribution to the ISMS, including the benefits of better security performance.
What happens if they do not conform to ISMS requirements.

sections.heading: 7.4 Communication
body: Decide what to communicate, when, with whom and how. Internal examples include policy updates and incident alerts. External examples include customer notifications and reports to regulators. A communication matrix is a common way to record this.

sections.heading: 7.5 Documented information
body: Documented information means information you must control and maintain, and the medium it is held on. It replaced the older terms 'documents' and 'records'.

You need the documented information ISO 27001 requires plus whatever you decide is necessary. When you create or update it, make sure it is identified, in a suitable format and reviewed and approved. Then control distribution, access, storage, version control, retention and disposal. This includes documents from outside, such as supplier contracts.

example.title: Competence versus awareness
example.text: A new firewall administrator needs competence: training on the firewall product and change process, with records kept. Every member of staff needs awareness: they know the policy exists, why it matters to them, and what happens if they ignore it.

exam_tips: Awareness has three points. Learn them as a set.
Version control, retention and disposal all sit under 7.5.

lessons.title: Clause 8: operation
lessons.intro: Clause 8 is where plans become routine. You run the processes, repeat risk assessments and carry out the treatment plan.

sections.heading: 8.1 Operational planning and control
body: Plan, implement and control the processes needed to meet requirements and carry out the actions from clause 6. Set criteria for those processes and run them to those criteria.

Keep documented information to show processes ran as planned. Control planned changes and review the consequences of unintended changes. Control externally provided processes, products or services that are relevant to the ISMS, such as outsourced IT.

sections.heading: 8.2 Risk assessment in operation
body: Perform risk assessments at planned intervals and when significant changes are proposed or occur. Keep the results.

sections.heading: 8.3 Risk treatment in operation
body: Implement the risk treatment plan. Keep the results.

example.title: Triggers for a new risk assessment
example.text: Your annual risk assessment is in January. In June the company moves its email to a new cloud provider. That is a significant change, so you assess the risk then, not next January.

exam_tips: Two triggers for risk assessment: planned intervals and significant change.
Clause 6 plans the risk work. Clause 8 does it and keeps the results.

lessons.title: Annex A and ISO/IEC 27002
lessons.intro: Annex A is the control list you cross-check against. ISO/IEC 27002 explains each control. This lesson shows how they fit together.

sections.heading: The four themes
points: 5 Organizational controls (37): policies, roles, assets, access, suppliers, incidents, continuity, compliance.
6 People controls (8): screening, employment terms, training, discipline, remote working, event reporting.
7 Physical controls (14): perimeters, entry, monitoring, equipment, media, utilities, disposal.
8 Technological controls (34): endpoints, access, malware, vulnerabilities, logging, networks, cryptography, development.

sections.heading: Annex A is not a mandatory checklist
body: You do not have to implement all 93 controls. You decide which controls your risks need, then compare with Annex A to check you have not missed any. Every Annex A control must appear in the Statement of Applicability with a decision: included and why, or excluded and why.

sections.heading: What ISO/IEC 27002 adds
body: For each control, 27002 gives a purpose and implementation guidance. It also tags each control with five attributes so you can filter and report on them:
points: Control type: preventive, detective, corrective.
Information security properties: confidentiality, integrity, availability.
Cybersecurity concepts: identify, protect, detect, respond, recover.
Operational capabilities: for example governance, asset management, identity and access management.
Security domains: governance and ecosystem, protection, defence, resilience.

sections.heading: The 11 new controls
body: 5.7 Threat intelligence, 5.23 Cloud services, 5.30 ICT readiness for business continuity, 7.4 Physical security monitoring, 8.9 Configuration management, 8.10 Information deletion, 8.11 Data masking, 8.12 Data leakage prevention, 8.16 Monitoring activities, 8.23 Web filtering, 8.28 Secure coding.
Use the Annex A screen and the flashcards to learn these.

example.title: Matching a control to a risk
example.text: Risk: developers copy live customer data into the test system. Relevant controls: 8.31 separation of development, test and production, 8.33 test information, and 8.11 data masking.

exam_tips: 114 controls was the 2013 figure. 93 is the 2022 figure.
The five cybersecurity concepts match the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions.

lessons.title: Mandatory documented information
lessons.intro: Auditors start with documents. Know which ones ISO 27001 explicitly requires and which clause asks for each.

sections.heading: Documents that define the ISMS
points: ISMS scope (4.3).
Information security policy (5.2).
Risk assessment process (6.1.2).
Risk treatment process (6.1.3).
Statement of Applicability (6.1.3 d).
Information security objectives (6.2).

sections.heading: Records that prove it works
points: Evidence of competence (7.2).
Evidence that processes ran as planned (8.1).
Risk assessment results (8.2).
Risk treatment results (8.3).
Monitoring and measurement results (9.1).
Audit programme and audit results (9.2).
Management review results (9.3).
Nonconformities, actions taken and results of corrective action (10.2).

sections.heading: The risk treatment plan
body: Most certification bodies treat the risk treatment plan as mandatory. The standard requires documented information about the risk treatment process (6.1.3) and its results (8.3).

sections.heading: Everything else
body: Clause 7.5.1 b lets you add any documented information you decide is necessary. Many Annex A controls also expect documents, such as documented operating procedures (5.37). Those are needed when the control is in your SoA.

example.title: Spot the extra
example.text: Which is not explicitly required by clauses 4 to 10: the ISMS scope, the security objectives, a network diagram, or management review results? The network diagram. It is useful, but no clause requires it.

exam_tips: Use the Documents checklist in Learn to test yourself on item and clause together.

lessons.title: Starting the ISMS project
lessons.intro: This lesson begins the implementation journey. Before any risk work starts, a Lead Implementer sets up the project properly.

sections.heading: Project charter
body: The charter authorises the ISMS project. It usually states objectives, scope, sponsor, roles, resources, budget, milestones and how progress will be reported. It gives the project manager formal authority.

sections.heading: Management commitment
body: Secure commitment early. Top management needs to understand the business case, such as customer demand for certification, regulatory pressure or reduced incident cost. Without commitment you will not get resources or decisions.

sections.heading: Interested parties
body: Start identifying interested parties and their requirements. This feeds the scope and later clause 4.2 work.

sections.heading: Gap analysis
body: Compare current practice with the requirements of ISO 27001 and, often, with Annex A. The output shows what exists, what is partial and what is missing. It shapes the project plan, budget and timeline.
A gap analysis does not certify anything and does not replace the risk assessment.

example.title: Gap analysis output
example.text: A gap analysis finds a security policy exists but has not been reviewed in three years, there is no risk assessment method, and access reviews happen informally. The plan schedules a policy review, a risk methodology workshop and a formal access review process.

exam_tips: The main purpose of a gap analysis is comparing current state with the standard.
TRECCERT's implementation outline starts with charter, commitment, interested parties, gap analysis.

lessons.title: Scope, policy, objectives and risk approach
lessons.intro: The establishment phase turns the project into an ISMS design. You set scope, policy and objectives, choose a risk method, plan the work and get sign-off.

sections.heading: Context and scope
body: Use the clause 4 outputs to draft the scope. Agree it with top management. Avoid a scope so narrow it means nothing to customers, or so wide the project cannot finish.

sections.heading: Policy and objectives
body: Draft the information security policy for top management to approve. Set objectives that are measurable where practicable and linked to the policy and risk results.

sections.heading: Risk assessment approach
body: Choose a method that gives consistent, valid and comparable results. ISO/IEC 27005:2022 describes two ways to identify risks:
points: Asset-based: list assets, then the threats and vulnerabilities for each.
Event-based: start from risk scenarios or events, often at a strategic level, without listing every asset.

sections.heading: Risk criteria
body: Define how you score likelihood and consequence, for example 1 to 5 each, and how scores combine into a risk level. Set the acceptance criteria: the level at or below which a risk owner can accept a risk without further treatment. Write these down before you assess, so results are comparable.

sections.heading: Implementation plan and authorisation
body: Create an implementation plan with tasks, owners, dates and resources. Then obtain formal management authorisation. Sign-off confirms commitment and resources, and is evidence of leadership under clause 5.1.

example.title: A simple risk matrix
example.text: Likelihood 1 to 5 multiplied by consequence 1 to 5 gives a score from 1 to 25. Criteria: 1 to 6 low, accept; 8 to 12 medium, treat or accept with risk owner sign-off; 15 to 25 high, must treat. A risk scored likelihood 4, consequence 4 is 16, so it is high and must be treated.

exam_tips: The method must give repeatable results. A method that depends on who runs it fails 6.1.2.
Management authorisation is not an Annex A control. It shows commitment and releases resources.

lessons.title: Risk treatment and the Statement of Applicability
lessons.intro: Risk treatment decides what you do about each risk. The Statement of Applicability records which controls you chose and why.

sections.heading: The four treatment options
body: These are commonly taught as four options, from the 2018 edition of ISO/IEC 27005:
points: Modify: apply controls to reduce likelihood or consequence.
Retain: accept the risk as it is, within the acceptance criteria.
Avoid: stop the activity that causes the risk.
Share: pass part of the consequence to another party, for example through insurance or a contract.

sections.heading: Choosing controls
body: For risks you modify, determine every control needed. Draw on any source: 27002, industry frameworks or your own design. Then compare your list with all 93 Annex A controls to check nothing necessary is missing.

sections.heading: Statement of Applicability
body: The SoA lists:
points: The necessary controls.
Why each is included.
Whether each is implemented.
Why any Annex A control is excluded.

sections.heading: Risk treatment plan and residual risk
body: The risk treatment plan sets out actions, owners, resources and dates. Risk owners approve it and accept the residual risk, which is the risk left after treatment.

sections.heading: Worked flow
points: Risk: laptop theft exposes customer data. Likelihood 3, consequence 4, score 12, medium.
Option: modify.
Controls: 8.1 user end point devices (full disk encryption), 8.24 use of cryptography, 6.7 remote working.
Residual score after controls: likelihood 3, consequence 1, score 3, low.
Risk owner signs the plan and accepts the residual risk.

example.title: Excluding a control
example.text: A fully remote firm with no offices excludes 7.1 physical security perimeters. The SoA justification reads: 'No company premises. Home working risks are covered by 6.7 Remote working and 7.9 Security of assets off-premises.'

exam_tips: Insurance is sharing. Stopping a service is avoiding. Accepting is retaining.
The SoA covers all 93 Annex A controls, not only the implemented ones.

lessons.title: Implementing controls and running the ISMS
lessons.intro: Implementation turns the treatment plan into working controls, trained people and controlled documents.

sections.heading: Policies and procedures
body: Write topic-specific policies where controls need them, such as access control, backup or acceptable use. Write procedures for repeatable tasks. Keep documents short enough that people follow them.

sections.heading: People
body: Screen staff in proportion to risk (6.1). Put security responsibilities in contracts (6.2). Train staff and refresh it regularly (6.3). Make sure there is a disciplinary process (6.4). Recover assets when people leave (5.11) and remove their access (5.18).

sections.heading: Competence, awareness and communication
body: Run an awareness programme for everyone and targeted training for key roles. Keep records. Follow the communication plan from 7.4.

sections.heading: Operating the ISMS
body: Once controls are live, the ISMS has to run as routine. Typical operating processes include access reviews, patching, backup tests, supplier reviews, incident handling and change management. Each needs an owner and evidence that it happens.

sections.heading: Incident management
body: Plan roles and procedures (5.24). Staff report events (6.8). Assess whether an event is an incident (5.25). Respond (5.26). Learn from it (5.27). Collect evidence properly when needed (5.28).

example.title: A leaver process
example.text: HR tells IT the leaving date. On the last day IT disables the accounts, and the manager collects the laptop and badge. HR reminds the leaver of their confidentiality duties. This one process uses controls 5.11, 5.18, 6.5 and 6.6.

exam_tips: Scenario questions often ask which control fits best. Use the Annex A search to check control names.

lessons.title: Monitoring and measurement
lessons.intro: You cannot show the ISMS works without measuring it. Clause 9.1 sets out what you must decide.

sections.heading: What 9.1 requires
body: Decide:
points: What to monitor and measure, including processes and controls.
Which methods give valid results. The 2022 edition notes results should be comparable and reproducible.
When to monitor and measure.
Who does it.
When results are analysed and evaluated.
Who analyses and evaluates them.

sections.heading: Good metrics
body: A useful metric is specific, measurable and linked to an objective or control. 'Percentage of critical patches applied within 14 days' is useful. 'Security is good' is not.

sections.heading: Evaluate both performance and effectiveness
body: You evaluate the security performance and the effectiveness of the ISMS. Keep the results as evidence. ISO/IEC 27004 gives guidance on designing measures.

example.title: A metric set
example.text: Objective: reduce phishing risk. Measures: training completion rate, phishing test click rate, number of reported suspicious emails. Collected monthly by the security team. Analysed quarterly by the ISMS manager. Reported to management review.

exam_tips: Know the 'what, how, when, who' structure of 9.1.
27004 is the measurement guidance standard.

lessons.title: Internal audit
lessons.intro: Internal audit checks that the ISMS meets your own requirements and ISO 27001, and that it works in practice.

sections.heading: What 9.2 requires
body: Carry out internal audits at planned intervals. Check that the ISMS conforms to the organisation's own requirements and to ISO 27001, and that it is effectively implemented and maintained.

sections.heading: The audit programme
body: Plan a programme covering frequency, methods, responsibilities, planning requirements and reporting. Take into account the importance of the processes and the results of previous audits. Define the criteria and scope of each audit.

sections.heading: Objectivity and impartiality
body: Choose auditors who are objective and impartial. They do not need to be external. They must not audit their own work.

sections.heading: Running an audit
body: ISO 19011 and ISO/IEC 27007 give guidance. A typical audit has these stages: plan, opening meeting, gather evidence through interviews, document review and observation, record findings, closing meeting, report, follow-up.
Report results to relevant management and keep evidence of the programme and the results.

example.title: A small company
example.text: A 40-person firm has one security manager. They cannot audit the security processes they run. The firm uses its finance manager, who is trained in auditing, to audit security. The security manager audits HR processes instead.

exam_tips: Objective and impartial does not mean external.
Programme planning considers process importance and previous results.

lessons.title: Management review
lessons.intro: Management review is where top management looks at the evidence and decides what to change.

sections.heading: Who and when
body: Top management reviews the ISMS at planned intervals to make sure it remains suitable, adequate and effective.

sections.heading: Inputs
points: Status of actions from previous reviews.
Changes in external and internal issues.
Changes in the needs and expectations of interested parties (added in 2022).
Feedback on security performance: nonconformities and corrective actions, monitoring results, audit results, objectives.
Feedback from interested parties.
Results of risk assessment and status of the risk treatment plan.
Opportunities for continual improvement.

sections.heading: Outputs
body: Decisions on continual improvement opportunities and any need for changes to the ISMS. Keep documented evidence of the results.

example.title: A review agenda
example.text: Item 1: actions from the last review. Item 2: new regulation on the horizon. Item 3: audit findings and corrective actions. Item 4: objective scorecard. Item 5: top risks and treatment status. Item 6: improvement proposals and decisions.

exam_tips: Management review is run by top management, not internal audit.
An agenda that mirrors the input list is good evidence.

lessons.title: Certification audits
lessons.intro: A Lead Implementer prepares the organisation for external certification. Know the stages and what happens to findings.

sections.heading: Who certifies
body: An accredited certification body audits against ISO 27001 and follows ISO/IEC 27006-1. In the UK, UKAS accredits certification bodies.

sections.heading: Stage 1
body: The certification body reviews documentation and readiness. It looks at scope, policy, risk process, SoA and whether internal audit and management review have run. It decides whether you are ready for Stage 2.

sections.heading: Stage 2
body: The certification body checks the ISMS is implemented and effective in practice. Auditors interview staff, sample records and observe controls.

sections.heading: Findings
points: Major nonconformity: a requirement is not met in a way that puts the ISMS's outcomes in doubt. Certification is withheld until the certification body accepts the correction and corrective action.
Minor nonconformity: a lapse that does not undermine the system. You submit a corrective action plan, and the next audit checks it.
Opportunity for improvement: a suggestion, not a failure.

sections.heading: The three-year cycle
body: The certificate lasts three years. Surveillance audits take place at least annually in years two and three. A recertification audit takes place before expiry.

example.title: A Stage 2 finding
example.text: The SoA says access reviews are quarterly. The auditor finds none have happened for nine months. That is likely a major nonconformity, because a key control is not operating. Certification waits until it is fixed and evidence is accepted.

exam_tips: Stage 1 is documents and readiness. Stage 2 is implementation and effectiveness.

lessons.title: Nonconformity and corrective action
lessons.intro: When something goes wrong, ISO 27001 wants you to fix it and stop it happening again.

sections.heading: Correction versus corrective action
body: Correction fixes the immediate problem. Corrective action removes the root cause so it does not recur. Exams test this difference often.

sections.heading: What 10.2 requires
points: React: control and correct it, and deal with the consequences.
Evaluate the need for action: review it, find the cause, and check whether similar nonconformities exist or could occur.
Implement any action needed.
Review the effectiveness of the corrective action.
Change the ISMS if needed.
Keep documented evidence of the nonconformity, actions taken and results.

sections.heading: Root cause analysis
body: Common techniques include the 5 Whys and the Ishikawa (fishbone) diagram. The standard does not require a specific technique. The aim is to find the system cause, not to blame a person.

sections.heading: Preventive action
body: ISO 27001:2013 removed the separate preventive action clause. Risk-based planning in clause 6 now does that job. TRECCERT's outline still uses the phrase 'corrective and preventive actions'.

example.title: 5 Whys
example.text: Finding: a leaver's account was still active after three weeks. Why? IT was not told. Why? HR emailed one person, who was on leave. Why? No shared mailbox or ticket was used. Why? The leaver process was never documented. Correction: disable the account. Corrective action: document the process, use a ticket queue, and check leaver accounts monthly.

exam_tips: Fixing it today is correction. Stopping it recurring is corrective action.
Effectiveness review is required, not optional.

lessons.title: Continual improvement
lessons.intro: The final lesson closes the loop. An ISMS is never finished.

sections.heading: 10.1 Continual improvement
body: Continually improve the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of the ISMS. In the 2022 edition, this subclause comes before nonconformity and corrective action.

sections.heading: Where improvements come from
points: Management review decisions.
Audit findings and opportunities for improvement.
Incidents and lessons learned (5.27).
Monitoring results and missed objectives.
Changes in threats, technology or business.

sections.heading: Communicating improvements
body: Tell the people affected what changed and why. This supports awareness under 7.3 and makes it more likely the change sticks.

example.title: Closing the loop
example.text: Monitoring shows phishing click rates have stopped falling. Management review approves a new reporting button and shorter monthly training. The change is planned under 6.3, communicated under 7.4, and measured again next quarter.

exam_tips: Suitability, adequacy and effectiveness: learn the three words together.
Clause 10 maps to Act in the PDCA convention.

questions.question: Which property is lost when an attacker alters payroll figures without being detected?
questions.explanation: Integrity concerns accuracy and completeness. Unauthorised change breaks integrity.

questions.question: A ransomware attack encrypts a file server so staff cannot open files. No data was copied out. Which property is affected?
questions.explanation: Staff cannot access or use the information, so availability is lost.

questions.question: Which standard in the 27000 family can an organisation be certified against?
questions.explanation: 27001 holds the requirements. The others are guidance.

questions.question: Where would you find the official definitions of ISMS terms?
questions.explanation: 27000 is the overview and vocabulary standard.

questions.question: What does the harmonized structure provide?
options: A common clause structure across ISO management system standards
questions.explanation: The shared structure lets organisations integrate 27001 with 9001, 42001 and others.

questions.question: Which standard provides requirements for bodies that certify ISMSs?
questions.explanation: 27006 covers certification body requirements. 27007 is audit guidance.

questions.question: How many controls are in Annex A of ISO/IEC 27001:2022?
questions.explanation: 93 controls in four themes. 114 was the 2013 figure.

questions.question: Which theme contains the most controls?
questions.explanation: Organizational has 37, Technological 34, Physical 14, People 8.

questions.question: Which clause requires top management to show leadership and commitment?
questions.explanation: 5.1 Leadership and commitment.

questions.question: Which clause was newly added in the 2022 edition?
questions.explanation: 6.3 requires changes to the ISMS to be planned.

questions.question: Which of these is a new control in 2022?
questions.explanation: 5.7 Threat intelligence is one of the 11 new controls.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a new 2022 control?
questions.explanation: 8.13 Information backup existed in 2013.

questions.question: Clause 4.2 requires the organisation to identify what?
options: Interested parties and their relevant requirements
questions.explanation: 4.2 covers needs and expectations of interested parties.

questions.question: Which item is mandatory documented information?
questions.explanation: 6.2 requires documented objectives. The others may be useful but are not explicitly required.

questions.question: Which 27002 attribute set uses Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover?
questions.explanation: These five concepts align with the NIST Cybersecurity Framework functions.

questions.question: Control 8.31 requires separation of which environments?
questions.explanation: 8.31 separates development, test and production.

questions.question: What did Amendment 1 (2024) add to ISO/IEC 27001:2022?
options: Climate change consideration in clauses 4.1 and 4.2
questions.explanation: The climate action amendment applied to many ISO management system standards.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of a gap analysis at project start?
options: Compare current practice with ISO 27001 requirements
questions.explanation: It shows what exists and what is missing, which shapes the project plan.

questions.question: Which input should the ISMS scope consider?
options: Issues from 4.1, requirements from 4.2, and interfaces and dependencies
questions.explanation: 4.3 lists these three inputs.

questions.question: Who establishes the information security policy?
questions.explanation: 5.2 places the policy with top management.

questions.question: The risk assessment process must produce results that are:
questions.explanation: 6.1.2 requires repeated assessments to give consistent, valid and comparable results.

questions.question: Which two sets of criteria must the risk assessment process establish?
options: Risk acceptance criteria and criteria for performing assessments
questions.explanation: Both are required by 6.1.2.

questions.question: Why is management authorisation obtained before implementation?
options: It is an Annex A control
To confirm commitment, resources and acceptance of the plan
questions.explanation: Formal sign-off secures resources and shows the leadership commitment 5.1 requires.

questions.question: Information security objectives must be:
options: Measurable where practicable and consistent with the policy
questions.explanation: 6.2 sets this requirement.

questions.question: A project charter for an ISMS project should mainly define:
options: Objectives, scope, sponsor, roles, resources and milestones
questions.explanation: The charter authorises and frames the project.

questions.question: Which risk treatment option is insurance an example of?
questions.explanation: Insurance transfers part of the consequence to a third party.

questions.question: An organisation stops offering a risky online service. Which option is this?
questions.explanation: Ending the activity removes the risk source.

questions.question: The SoA must contain:
options: Necessary controls, justification for inclusion, implementation status, and justification for excluding Annex A controls
questions.explanation: 6.1.3 d sets these contents.

questions.question: Why must the organisation compare its controls with Annex A?
options: Every Annex A control is mandatory
To check no necessary controls are overlooked
questions.explanation: Annex A is a checklist. Controls can be excluded with justification.

questions.question: Who approves the risk treatment plan?
questions.explanation: Risk owners approve it and accept residual risk under 6.1.3.

questions.question: Clause 7.3 Awareness requires people to know:
options: The policy, their contribution, and consequences of not conforming
questions.explanation: These three points form 7.3.

questions.question: When must risk assessments be repeated under 8.2?
options: At planned intervals and when significant changes occur
questions.explanation: Both triggers are required.

questions.question: Which control best addresses an employee leaving with a company laptop?
questions.explanation: 5.11 covers recovering assets on leaving.

questions.question: Which control applies to background checks on new staff?
questions.explanation: 6.1 Screening.

questions.question: A company stores customer data in a SaaS platform. Which new control is most directly relevant?
questions.explanation: 5.23 Information security for use of cloud services.

questions.question: Clause 7.5 controls documented information. Which is part of that control?
questions.explanation: 7.5.3 covers version control, retention and disposal among others.

questions.question: Internal audits must be carried out by auditors who are:
questions.explanation: 9.2 requires objectivity and impartiality, not external status.

questions.question: Which is an input to management review?
options: Results of risk assessment and status of risk treatment
questions.explanation: 9.3 lists risk assessment results and treatment status as inputs.

questions.question: What does Stage 1 of the certification audit mainly assess?
questions.explanation: Stage 1 reviews documentation and readiness. Stage 2 tests implementation.

questions.question: How often are surveillance audits normally held?
questions.explanation: Surveillance audits happen yearly between certification and recertification.

questions.question: Clause 9.1 requires the organisation to determine:
options: What to monitor and measure, methods, timing and who analyses results
questions.explanation: These are the 9.1 requirements.

questions.question: Who conducts the management review?
questions.explanation: 9.3 places the review with top management.

questions.question: Which standard gives guidance on monitoring and measurement?
questions.explanation: 27004 covers monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation.

questions.question: An auditor finds a firewall rule review was missed. The team completes the review that day. This is:
questions.explanation: Fixing the immediate issue is correction. Corrective action addresses why it was missed.

questions.question: What must happen after corrective action is implemented?
questions.explanation: 10.2 requires effectiveness review.

questions.question: In ISO/IEC 27001:2022, what is the title of clause 10.1?
questions.explanation: The 2022 edition reordered clause 10. 10.1 is Continual improvement and 10.2 is Nonconformity and corrective action. Preventive action was removed in 2013, and management review is 9.3.

questions.question: Continual improvement in clause 10.1 targets the ISMS's:
questions.explanation: 10.1 requires continual improvement of the ISMS's suitability, adequacy and effectiveness.

questions.question: Why check whether similar nonconformities exist elsewhere?
options: To find wider weaknesses and prevent recurrence
questions.explanation: 10.2 requires this check as part of corrective action.

questions.question: Which PDCA stage does clause 10 represent?
questions.explanation: By convention, improvement is the Act stage. The standard itself does not mention PDCA.

questions.question: What evidence must be kept for nonconformities?
options: Nature of the nonconformity, actions taken and results of corrective action
questions.explanation: 10.2 requires this documented information.

questions.question: Which is an output of management review?
options: Decisions on improvement opportunities and any changes needed to the ISMS
The risk acceptance criteria for the first time
questions.explanation: 9.3 outputs include improvement decisions and any need for changes to the ISMS.

questions.question: Who should internal audit results be reported to?
questions.explanation: 9.2 requires results to be reported to relevant management.

questions.question: An audit programme under 9.2 must take into account:
options: The importance of the processes concerned and the results of previous audits
questions.explanation: Programme planning considers process importance and previous audit results.

questions.question: Which is the best example of a measurable ISMS metric under 9.1?
options: Percentage of staff completing awareness training within 30 days of joining
questions.explanation: A useful metric is specific and measurable, so trends can be analysed and evaluated.

questions.question: During Stage 2, the auditor finds a major nonconformity. What normally happens?
options: Certification is withheld until correction and corrective action are accepted
The certificate is issued with a note
questions.explanation: A major nonconformity must be addressed, with evidence accepted by the certification body, before certification is granted.

questions.question: Can an internal auditor audit their own work?
options: No, it breaches objectivity and impartiality
questions.explanation: 9.2 requires auditors who ensure objectivity and impartiality. Auditing your own work undermines both.

questions.question: Which standard gives guidance specific to auditing an ISMS?
questions.explanation: 27007 gives ISMS audit guidance, building on ISO 19011.
